articles.title: I built a fully local alternative to Wispr Flow in Rust
articles.excerpt: I wanted dictation like Wispr Flow, but without the subscription and without my voice being uploaded to someone's cloud. So I built Hamsa, and it is now open source. How it works Hold Ctrl + Win, spea…
articles.body: I wanted dictation like Wispr Flow, but without the subscription and without my voice being uploaded to someone's cloud. So I built Hamsa, and it is now open source. How it works Hold Ctrl + Win, speak, let go, and the text is pasted into whatever app has focus. Your editor, a chat, a browser, an email, anywhere you can type. Double-tap the shortcut instead and it keeps listening hands-free: tap once to finish, Esc to cancel. While you speak, your words appear live above a small floating bar. Everything runs on your PC The speech engine is called Phonon, a pure Rust implementation of the Parakeet-TDT model. It runs on your GPU through wgpu when one is available, with a CPU path if not. No account, no subscription, and your voice and words are never uploaded.

articles.title: I built a Fortnite-style DBNO revive plugin for Minecraft (Paper 1.21)
articles.excerpt: Death in Minecraft survival servers is binary you die, your items scatter, your XP evaporates. I wanted Fortnite-style "down but not out" (DBNO) mechanics, so I built it as a Paper 1.21.x plugin. How…
articles.body: Death in Minecraft survival servers is binary you die, your items scatter, your XP evaporates. I wanted Fortnite-style "down but not out" (DBNO) mechanics, so I built it as a Paper 1.21.x plugin. How it works Lethal damage puts the player into a downed state: forced crawl, a bleed-out boss bar, no item drops yet. A teammate sneak-holding next to them revives them (a few seconds channel configurable). An enemy can hold sneak to execute, or the timer runs out real death. Heart/item effects only fire on real death, so lifesteal SMP mechanics stay correct. The plugin is small on purpose: one config.yml, one messages.yml, no dependencies beyond Paper.

articles.body: Apple publishes written App Store reviews as a public customer-review feed, one storefront at a time. There is no official bulk "all countries" API, so a US row and a UK row of the same app are different records. If you want a spreadsheet you can filter by country, you fetch each storefront and merge the results. This is a short guide to doing that and opening the result in CSV, Excel or Google Sheets. At the end I use an Apify actor I built that loops the storefronts, caps the cost, and lets you download the dataset as a spreadsheet. Disclosure: I work on CleanFeed Data, and that actor is ours. You can also call Apple's feed yourself with curl ; I walked through that in an earlier tutorial . What you'll need A free Apify account (the free plan includes $5 of usage each month).

articles.title: Ratchet: A Closed-Loop Verification Gate That Turns PRDs into Live Browser Proof
articles.excerpt: AI coding agents are great at writing code, but they love saying "it's done" the moment unit tests pass—without ever checking if the app actually works in a real browser. To fix that, I built Ratchet:…
articles.body: AI coding agents are great at writing code, but they love saying "it's done" the moment unit tests pass—without ever checking if the app actually works in a real browser. To fix that, I built Ratchet : a closed-loop verification gate powered by Kane CLI that refuses to lock a build until 100% of your PRD's acceptance criteria are proven in a live browser. How the Closed Loop Works Instead of relying on an agent's self-reported completion, Ratchet drives Kane CLI headlessly and enforces a strict verification flow: Spec Sync: Reads the project's PRD and syncs acceptance criteria against Kane CLI's structured design and coverage state ( kane-cli cover gaps --json ), including safe no-op handling when the design is already up to date.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space .

articles.body: Explore This Section Science Citizen Science Amateur Astronomer? Be a… Overview Resources Opportunities Citizen Science Highlights About Science Activation Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova . These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s Kilonova Catcher project! Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network.

articles.body: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft. The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.

articles.title: 1st-ever detection of a dying star's 'final nuclear heartbeat' challenges what we know about our sun's eventual death
articles.excerpt: Astronomers have caught a rare transitional phase at the end of a star's life, a fossilized remnant of stellar death throes, that could change our picture of the sun's final days.
articles.body: As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper. New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed.
articles.author: Robert Lea

articles.title: Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
articles.excerpt: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is add…
articles.body: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network . Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers. As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening.
